newsitem.title: UK: EMS/Marks stays firm as German govt comments eyed.
newsitem.headline: EMS/Marks stays firm as German govt comments eyed.

text.p: The mark was firmer on its European cross rates on Wednesday as traders awaited comments from the German government on the strength of the currency following today's regular cabinet meeting.
Speaking to reporters late Tuesday, Finance Minister Theo Waigel said he would make a statement to the cabint on the need for a strong mark and a strong single European currency.
Government sources said Wednesday no formal statement was likely but officials would comment on foreign exchange market developments at a press conference after the cabinet meeting about 1230 GMT.

"I'm not sure Waigel can say much more than he has already on this issue and, as a result, the bounce of the mark has been pretty limited," said Michael Burke, economist at Citibank. "It's really just wait and see at this stage."

Earlier on Tuesday, Waigel said the recent slide of the mark, against the dollar and sterling in particular, was an overreaction and Germany was in close contact with other members of the Group of Seven industrialised nations (G7) on the issue.
The German government is interested in a strong mark and a strong euro, Waigel said. Analysts said traders are now more wary about the possibility of central bank intervention.

"If the comments boost expectations of intervention they could have a major impact, but it would really just buy time because the domestic German recovery is still pretty fragile," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International. "The fact that the mark has already given back half of its gains already today suggests the market is prepared to push it weaker regardless."

Lyons said the Bundesbank tends to intervene at major market turning points and he believes there is not yet sufficient reason to believe the mark is at such a turning point. As a result, any intervention may well prove unsuccessful, he said.
Analysts said intervention to buy marks would only be effective if backed up shortly by a rise in German interest rates but said that this was unlikely for now at least.

Short-term interest rate futures contracts, however, edged lower this week, indicating the market has become slightly more wary about the prospect of tighter German monetary policy in response to a continued slide in the mark.

"The Bundesbank has a lot of political capital with the market and its verbal intervention will help support the mark. But an interest rate rise would be ridiculous at this stage with unemployment over four million," said Burke at Citibank.
The mark's decline has been driven by concern that the new euro, which is planned to replace the mark in 1999, will include traditionally less-stable currencies like the Italian lira.

Prevailing expectations that European economic and monetary union will have a broad-based membership and start on time means the mark has not weakened significantly against other potential EMU participants like the French franc, the Spanish peseta and the Italian lira.
Concerns about the stability of the new euro has, however, seen funds flow to non-EMU units like the dollar, sterling and even the Swiss franc.
At 0930 GMT, mark/French franc was at 3.3788/90 compared with 3.3764/69 on Tuesday and an early high at 3.3803. Mark/lira was 972.50/75 versus 970.95/25 yesterday and a high at 973.45.
Elsewhere, the Norwegian crown firmed to 4.1700/30 per mark from 4.1920 on Tuesday after Norway's central bank raised its key overnight lending rate to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent.

Analysts said the move partly reverses rate cuts earlier in the year, which were aimed at capping a soaring crown. The crown has weakened since and this has allowed rates to return to more appropriate levels, they said.
